retained_pairs.rationale: Acts names the hurricane wind Euraquilo rushing from the island; Jonah describes a great sea surge after the Lord stirs up wind, threatening the ship. The maritime danger corresponds, while the named wind and stated divine agency differ. Paul is not assigned Jonah's flight or made the narrated cause of this storm.

retained_pairs.rationale: Acts says the ship cannot face the wind and gives way to being driven; Jonah says the men strain to return to land but cannot as the sea grows fiercer. Both depict failed resistance to storm conditions, with different attempted maneuvers and no identical course or crew inferred.

Acts reports cargo thrown overboard after violent storm battering; Jonah reports equipment thrown into the sea to lighten the load. The shared unloading response has different stated objects. Jonah's explicit lightening purpose and Acts' next-day timing remain in their respective accounts, rather than identifying the cargo as a particular commodity.

Acts specifically names the ship's tackle being thrown overboard by their own hands on the third day; Jonah names equipment thrown into the sea to lighten the load. The equipment disposal corresponds without making every item identical or adding Acts' day count and hand-action wording to Jonah.

Acts describes many days without sun or stars and the loss of remaining hope of rescue. The psalm describes storm-tossed mariners' melting courage, swallowed-up wisdom and cry to the Lord. These depict maritime desperation; the psalm's prayer and narrated rescue are not inserted into this particular Acts verse or its weather details.

Acts explicitly says the ship was lightened by throwing grain into the sea after the people had eaten. Jonah describes equipment thrown into the sea to lighten the load. The common purpose coexists with different objects; only Acts here places disposal after eating. Jonah's equipment is not called grain, and the disposals remain separate voyages.
